title: How the money works
summary: Who pays whom in affiliate marketing, how payouts are calculated, which verticals are regulated and how networks approve, hold and pay. By the end you can read an offer page line by line and choose a sensible first offer.

lessons.title: What affiliate marketing is
objectives: By the end you can explain affiliate marketing in one plain sentence.
You can name the five players in every deal and what each one wants.
You can follow one result from ad to payout and see where money is made or lost.

steps.h: You are paid for results you send
steps.p: Affiliate marketing is a simple deal. A company pays you a fee when a person you sent does something the company values, such as signing up, making a first deposit or buying a product. You pay for the attention that brings those people. Your profit is the gap between the two.
steps.more: This is why affiliate work is often called performance marketing. Nobody pays you for effort, likes or nice-looking ads. You are paid when a measurable action happens and the company accepts it as valid. That makes the model fair to the company, because it only pays for results. It also moves most of the risk onto you, because you spend money on ads before you know whether any results will come. Everything you learn in VooSquare Academy is about managing that one gap well: buying attention at a price that leaves room for profit, and sending people who are genuinely right for the offer.

d.s: You buy the attention that creates it

steps.say: Let's start with the whole deal in one idea. A company pays you a fee when a person you sent does something the company values, like signing up, making a first deposit, or buying a product. Meanwhile, you pay for the attention that brings those people. Your profit is the gap between the two. Nobody pays you for effort, likes or nice-looking ads. You're paid for measurable results, and because you spend before results come, most of the risk sits with you.

steps.h: The five players in every deal
steps.p: Every affiliate deal involves the same five players. Once you know what each one wants, most of the rules, payment delays and disputes you meet later will make sense, because each rule protects one of these players from another.
d: Advertiser|owns the product and pays for results
Affiliate|you, sending people to the offer
User|the real person who decides to act
steps.say: Every affiliate deal involves the same five players, and they're on the cards. The advertiser owns the product and pays for results. The network connects advertisers with affiliates. The affiliate is you, sending people to the offer. The traffic source sells you attention. And the user is the real person who decides to act. Once you know what each one wants, most rules, payment delays and disputes will make sense, because each rule protects one player from another.

steps.p: The advertiser is the company that owns the product: a broker, a sportsbook, a bank app, an online shop. It pays for new customers it can keep. It sets the payout, the countries it accepts and the rules for what counts as a valid customer.
steps.more: Advertisers are also called merchants, brands or offer owners. They use affiliates because they only pay when results arrive, so their marketing cost is predictable. In return they protect themselves with rules: the customer must be new, from an accepted country, of legal age, and sometimes must deposit a minimum amount or verify their identity. If your users do not meet those rules, the advertiser will not pay for them. Keep that in mind every time you read an offer.

d.s: Wants customers worth more than they cost

steps.say: The advertiser is the company that owns the product: a broker, a sportsbook, a bank app, or an online shop. It pays for new customers it can keep. So it sets the payout, the countries it accepts, and the rules for what counts as a valid customer. For example, the customer may need to be new, of legal age, from an accepted country, and sometimes verified. If your users don't meet those rules, the advertiser won't pay for them.

steps.h: The network sits in the middle
steps.p: Most beginners work through an affiliate network. The network signs deals with many advertisers, gives you tracking links, counts your results and pays you. It keeps a margin between what the advertiser pays it and what it pays you.
steps.more: A network saves you from negotiating with dozens of companies one by one. You get one account, one dashboard and one payment. Your main contact there is the affiliate manager, who can explain offers, raise caps and sometimes improve payouts once you prove quality. Some advertisers also run their own in-house programmes, called direct deals. Direct deals can pay more because there is no middle margin, but they usually expect experience and steady volume before they accept you.
steps.say: Most beginners work through an affiliate network, and you can see it sitting in the middle of this flow. The network signs deals with many advertisers, gives you tracking links, counts your results and pays you. It keeps a margin between what the advertiser pays it and what it pays you. In return, you get one account, one dashboard, one payment, and usually an affiliate manager who can explain offers and raise caps.

steps.p: As the affiliate, you choose the offer, the country, the audience, the ad and the page people land on. You pay the traffic source up front and earn back only when results are approved. Know clearly which parts of the deal are yours to change.
steps.say: Now, you, the affiliate. Look at the two columns. You control which offer you promote, the geo and audience, your ads and landing page, and your daily budget. You don't control the payout rate, the advertiser's quality rules, the platform's ad review, or the user's decision. Know clearly which parts are yours to change. You pay the traffic source up front, and earn back only when results are approved.

steps.p: A traffic source is any place that sells you the attention of people: Meta, TikTok, Google, a native ad network or a Telegram channel owner. It is paid whether or not anyone converts. Its rules decide what you are allowed to advertise and how.
steps.more: This is the most important fact about the cost side of the business. The platform charges you for impressions or clicks, not for deposits. If your ad gets a thousand clicks and nobody signs up, you still pay for the thousand clicks. Each traffic source also has its own advertising policies. Trading, gambling, finance and health are restricted on most big platforms and may need written permission or verification before you can run ads. The Traffic 101 module covers traffic sources in detail.

d.s: The source earns on every view or click

steps.say: A traffic source is any place that sells you people's attention: Meta, TikTok, Google, a native ad network, or a Telegram channel owner. Here's the most important fact on the cost side. It's paid whether or not anyone converts. If your ad gets a thousand clicks and nobody signs up, you still pay for the thousand clicks. Its rules also decide what you're allowed to advertise, and trading, gambling, finance and health are restricted on most big platforms.

steps.h: The user is a real person
steps.p: The user is the person who sees your ad and decides to act. Every other player only earns if that person is treated honestly. Misleading users leads to rejected ads, banned accounts and conversions reversed when the advertiser sees poor quality customers.

d.text: If a deal only works by misleading people, it will fail later and cost more. Honest ads are the only kind that last.

steps.h: Follow one result from ad to cash
steps.p: Here is the path of one result. Each arrow is a place where a person can drop off, a result can go untracked or money can be delayed. Later modules teach you how to protect each step.
steps.more: The user sees your ad and taps it. Your tracking link records the click with a unique click ID, then sends the user to the offer or to your own page first. The user signs up and deposits. The advertiser's system records that the click ID converted and tells the network. The network shows the conversion in your dashboard, usually as pending. After the advertiser checks quality, it becomes approved, and you are paid on the network's schedule. If the click ID is lost anywhere on that path, the advertiser may have a customer and you may get no credit.
steps.say: Follow one result from ad to cash along this flow. The ad is shown. Someone clicks. They reach a landing page. They sign up or deposit. The network records it. And you get paid. Each arrow is a place where a person can drop off, a result can go untracked, or money can be delayed. Behind the scenes, your tracking link records a unique click I D, and if that I D is lost anywhere, you may get no credit.

steps.p: Here is that path as a system. Watch the dots: people move from left to right, and data moves back from the advertiser to the network. If the click ID drops off anywhere on this map, the result can be real and still not be credited to you.
steps.more: Read the map in two directions. Forward is the user: ad, tracking link, offer page, sign-up, deposit. Backward is the data: the advertiser records the deposit against the click ID and tells the network with a message called a postback. The network then shows it in your dashboard as pending, approves it after its checks, and pays you on its schedule. You only control the left side of the map, so you protect it by testing your tracking link before you spend. Full setup: Tracking setup lab module.

steps.p: Your profit on a campaign is what the network pays you minus what you paid the traffic source. Tools, creatives and your time are costs too, and you should add them later. Start by getting this one line right every single day.
steps.say: Profit is simple arithmetic, and the formula's on screen: approved payouts, minus ad spend, equals profit. Notice the word approved. Tools, creatives and your time are costs too, and you'll add them later. For now, start by getting this one line right every single day.

steps.p: Example: you spend $200 on ads in a week. The network approves 5 conversions at $50 each, which is $250. Your profit is $50 before other costs. Your return on spend is $50 divided by $200, which is 25%.
steps.more: Now look at how thin that is. If the advertiser rejects just one of the five conversions, you receive 4 × $50 = $200, exactly what you spent. Your profit drops to zero. If two are rejected, you lose $50. This is why approved results matter more than results shown on day one, and why later lessons spend so much time on quality, offer rules and tracking. All figures here are an example to show the arithmetic, not a forecast.

d.text: $250 payouts − $200 spend = $50 profit. One rejected conversion turns it into $0.

steps.say: Let's try an example week. You spend two hundred dollars on ads. The network approves five conversions at fifty dollars each, which is two hundred and fifty dollars. If the advertiser rejects just one of the five, you get two hundred dollars, and your profit drops to zero. These figures are an example, not a forecast.

steps.h: Common beginner mistakes, and the fix
steps.p: These five mistakes cost most new affiliates their first budget. Each one has a simple fix. Read them now so you recognise them when they tempt you, because every one of them feels reasonable in the moment.
d: Counting pending as profit|plan with approved payouts only
Ignoring costs beyond ads|add tools and creatives every week
Treating likes as results|you are paid for actions, not reactions
Promising results in ads|honest ads only; misleading ones get rejected
Skipping the offer rules|read who counts as valid before you spend
steps.say: These five mistakes cost most new affiliates their first budget, and each has a simple fix. Counting pending as profit, so plan with approved payouts only. Promising results in ads, when honest ads are the only kind that last. And skipping the offer rules, so read who counts as valid before you spend.

lessons.title: Payout models: CPA, CPL, RevShare and more
objectives: By the end you can define CPA, CPL, RevShare, hybrid and CPI deals in plain words.
You can calculate what you would earn under each model from a simple example.
You can choose a payout model that fits a small budget and explain why.

steps.h: How you are paid shapes everything
steps.p: The payout model is the rule for when and how much you earn. It decides how fast cash comes back to you, how much risk you carry and what your ads should aim for. Five models cover almost every deal you will see.

d.s: CPA, CPL, RevShare, hybrid and CPI

steps.say: The payout model is the rule for when and how much you earn. It decides how fast cash comes back to you, how much risk you carry, and what your ads should aim for. Five models cover almost every deal you'll see: C P A, C P L, RevShare, hybrid, and C P I. We'll take them one at a time.

steps.h: The five models at a glance
steps.p: Here is the whole picture before we go through each model one by one. Notice the last column. How fast money returns to you matters a lot when your budget is small and you need cash to keep testing.

rows: A set action, often a deposit

steps.say: Here's the whole picture first. C P A pays for a set action, often a deposit, and cash comes back in weeks. C P L pays for a qualified lead, in weeks, but in small sums. RevShare pays a share of user revenue that builds over months. Hybrid is a fixed fee plus a share, so some now and some later. And C P I pays per app install. Notice that last column. When your budget is small, cash speed matters a lot.

steps.more: The figures match the worked examples later in this lesson: $40 CPA, 30% RevShare, or a hybrid of $25 plus 15%. Not every network offers every model on every offer, and RevShare or hybrid deals are often only opened after you show steady volume. Layouts and names vary by network; read your own offer page. steps.h: CPA: a fixed fee per action
steps.p: CPA means cost per action, sometimes called cost per acquisition. The advertiser pays a fixed amount when a user completes a defined action. In trading and iGaming that action is usually a first-time deposit, called an FTD. The offer page says exactly what counts.
steps.more: Read the definition carefully, because the word action hides details. Many offers only pay for an FTD above a minimum deposit amount. Some only pay for qualified FTDs, where the user must also verify their identity or place a certain amount of activity. The user must be new to that advertiser, located in an accepted country and of legal age. People in the industry sometimes write CPFTD, cost per first-time deposit, to be precise. Once a CPA is approved, it is yours, no matter what the user does next. That certainty is why most beginners start with CPA.

d.s: Usually the FTD in trading and iGaming

steps.say: C P A means cost per action, sometimes called cost per acquisition. The advertiser pays a fixed amount when a user completes a defined action. In trading and iGaming, that action is usually a first-time deposit, called an F T D. Read the definition carefully, because there may be a minimum deposit, or extra checks like identity verification. Once a C P A is approved, it's yours, whatever the user does next. That certainty is why most beginners start here.

steps.p: Example: an offer pays $40 per qualified FTD. Over a month, 12 of your users make qualifying deposits and the advertiser approves all 12. You earn $480, whatever those users do afterwards. Your profit is $480 minus your ad spend.
steps.say: Let's work an example. An offer pays forty dollars per qualified F T D. Over a month, twelve of your users make qualifying deposits, and the advertiser approves all twelve. Follow the sum on screen: twelve times forty is four hundred and eighty dollars, whatever those users do afterwards. Your profit is that four hundred and eighty, minus your ad spend.

steps.p: CPL means cost per lead. You are paid when a user submits details, such as a name, email or phone number, that pass the advertiser's checks. Payouts are smaller than CPA because a lead is earlier in the journey. Quality checks are often strict.
steps.more: Lead offers come in two common forms. Single opt-in, or SOI, pays when the user submits the form once. Double opt-in, or DOI, pays only after the user confirms, for example by clicking a link sent to their email. DOI pays more because the lead is more likely real. Example: a CPL offer pays $3 per lead. You send 100 leads, and 20 are rejected as duplicates or fake numbers. You are paid 80 × $3 = $240. Lead offers are easy to start but punish low quality, so never use incentives or fake forms to inflate numbers.

d.s: Fake or duplicate leads are rejected

steps.say: C P L means cost per lead. You're paid when a user submits details, like a name, email or phone number, that pass the advertiser's checks. Payouts are smaller than C P A, because a lead is earlier in the journey. Quality checks are often strict, and fake or duplicate leads are rejected. So never use incentives or fake forms to inflate numbers. Lead offers are easy to start, but they punish low quality.

steps.h: Try it: what can you pay per CPL lead?
steps.p: A CPL offer pays $3 per approved lead. In your geo, the manager says about 80% of leads are approved. You want to keep a 20% margin. Work out the most you can pay for each lead you send, then check your answer.
steps.more: Each lead you send is worth $3 × 80% = $2.40, because one in five is rejected. That is your break-even. Keeping a 20% margin leaves $2.40 × 0.8 = $1.92 as the most you should pay per lead. Figures are an example.

steps.h: RevShare: a share of what users bring
steps.p: RevShare means revenue share. You receive a percentage of the net revenue the advertiser earns from your users, for as long as the deal says. Example: the chart compares one group of users paid on CPA with the same group paid on RevShare.
steps.more: In this example, the CPA deal pays $480 once in month one and nothing after. The RevShare deal starts lower but keeps adding while users stay active, passing the CPA total in month seven. The numbers are invented to show the shape, and real results can be much lower or higher. Net revenue is usually what users deposited or lost to the advertiser, minus costs such as bonuses, payment fees and sometimes taxes. Each programme defines it differently. If users win more than they lose in a month, net revenue can be negative.
steps.say: RevShare means revenue share. You receive a percentage of the net revenue the advertiser earns from your users, for as long as the deal says. Look at the chart. It's an example comparing one group of users paid on C P A with the same group on RevShare. The C P A line pays four hundred and eighty dollars once. The RevShare line starts lower but keeps adding, passing it in month seven. These numbers are invented to show the shape, and real results can be much lower or higher.

steps.h: Read how net revenue is defined
steps.p: RevShare is only as good as its terms. They say what is deducted before your share is calculated, how long you earn, and what happens in a month when the advertiser loses money on your users. Read those three points before you accept.
steps.more: Negative carryover means a negative month is carried forward and subtracted from your future earnings until it is paid off. Some programmes reset each month, which is better for you. Lifetime RevShare pays for as long as users stay active. Others stop after a fixed period, such as 12 or 24 months. RevShare also depends on the advertiser reporting honestly, because you cannot see their accounts. Work with established networks and keep your own records.

d.text: Before choosing RevShare, ask: what is deducted, how long does it last, and is there negative carryover?

steps.say: RevShare is only as good as its terms. Before you accept, read three points: what's deducted before your share is worked out, how long you earn, and what happens in a month when the advertiser loses money on your users. That last one is called negative carryover, where a negative month is subtracted from your future earnings. The warning on screen gives you the three questions to ask, every time.

steps.h: Hybrid: a fee now plus a share later
steps.p: A hybrid deal pays a smaller fixed amount per action plus a smaller RevShare percentage. It balances cash today with income later. Networks often offer hybrids to affiliates who have already shown steady volume and good user quality.
steps.more: Example: instead of $40 CPA, a network offers a hybrid of $25 per FTD plus 15% RevShare. On 20 FTDs you get $500 up front instead of $800. If those users generate $3,000 of net revenue over six months, the RevShare part adds $450, so the hybrid total is $950. If they generate only $1,000, the hybrid total is $650 and pure CPA would have been better. A hybrid is a bet that your users are worth more over time than the CPA price.

d.s: Some cash now, some later

steps.say: A hybrid deal pays a smaller fixed amount per action, plus a smaller RevShare percentage. It balances cash today with income later. Networks often offer hybrids to affiliates who've already shown steady volume and good user quality. Think of a hybrid as a bet that your users are worth more over time than the C P A price. If they're not, pure C P A would have paid better.

steps.p: CPI means cost per install. You are paid when a user installs and opens an app, as measured by the app's tracking tool. Payouts per install are small, so CPI suits large volumes of cheap traffic. Many offers also require an action inside the app, such as registration.
steps.more: Apps usually count installs through a mobile measurement partner, or MMP, a third-party tool that records which ad or affiliate link led to each install. Some app offers pay on a later event instead, such as a completed registration or first purchase, often written as CPA or CPE (cost per event). Install fraud, where fake devices install apps, is common across the industry, so advertisers check closely and reject suspicious traffic.

d.s: Often with an in-app event required

steps.say: C P I means cost per install. You're paid when a user installs and opens an app, as measured by the app's tracking tool. Payouts per install are small, so C P I suits large volumes of cheap traffic. Many offers also require an action inside the app, like registration. Install fraud, with fake devices installing apps, is common, so advertisers check closely and reject suspicious traffic.

steps.p: These are the two main choices in trading and iGaming. Neither is better in general. The right one depends on how much cash you have, how patient you can be and how much you trust the advertiser to report fairly.

a.title: CPA
items: Easier to fund the next test

b.title: RevShare
items: Can pay after you stop spending

steps.say: These are the two main choices in trading and iGaming, so compare the columns. C P A brings cash back within weeks, with a fixed, known value per F T D, but strict qualification rules, and it's easier to fund your next test. RevShare builds cash over months, its value depends on user activity, it relies on honest reporting, and it can keep paying after you stop spending. Neither is better in general. It depends on your cash, your patience, and your trust in the advertiser.

steps.p: Example: you send 20 FTDs. Here is what three different deals could pay in month one and after six months. The RevShare figures assume $500 of net revenue in month one and $3,000 over six months. They are invented to show the arithmetic.
steps.more: CPA: 20 × $40 = $800, paid once. RevShare at 30%: month one is 30% of $500 = $150, and after six months it is 30% of $3,000 = $900. Hybrid at $25 plus 15%: month one is (20 × $25) + 15% of $500 = $500 + $75 = $575, and after six months it is $500 + 15% of $3,000 = $500 + $450 = $950. Notice that the CPA deal gives the most cash early. A beginner who needs money back to keep testing is usually better off taking it.

steps.h: A vertical is a type of offer
steps.p: A vertical is a group of offers that sell the same kind of thing to the same kind of person. Trading, iGaming, finance, sweepstakes, nutra, e-commerce and apps are the common ones. Each has its own payouts, users, rules and risks.

d.s: Each vertical has its own rules

steps.p: Trading offers pay you to bring people who open and fund an account with a broker or trading platform. Payouts can be high because each depositing user can be valuable. The products are risky, many users lose money, and rules are strict.
steps.more: Trading offers include forex, CFDs, stocks, crypto and other instruments. Some products, such as binary options, are banned for ordinary retail customers in a number of countries. Brokers are licensed by financial regulators, and a licence in one country does not automatically allow them to take customers from another. Major ad platforms have financial services policies, and in some countries they require advertisers to be verified or licensed before running these ads. Your ads must never promise profits or hide risk. Check the platform's current financial services policy and local law for every country you target.

steps.p: Finance offers include loans, credit cards, savings and banking apps, insurance and payment apps. Users often compare options carefully, so clear ads work best. Many countries regulate how credit and investment products are advertised, including required wording on cost and risk.

steps.h: Sweepstakes: clear terms or skip it
steps.p: Sweepstakes offers ask users to enter a prize draw, usually by giving an email or phone number. They pay per lead and convert easily, which also makes them a magnet for misleading ads. Some funnels lead to hidden subscriptions or charges.
steps.more: Consumer protection laws in many countries require prize promotions to state clearly who runs them, how winners are chosen and what the user agrees to. A sweepstakes offer that signs users up to paid SMS services or recurring charges without clear consent is a scam, whatever the payout. Platforms also reject ads that imply someone has already won. If you promote sweepstakes, choose offers with transparent terms and make sure your ad describes exactly what the user is entering.

steps.p: Nutra is short for nutraceuticals: supplements, diet, beauty and wellness products. Payouts can be attractive, and so is the temptation to make health claims. Ads that promise cures, weight-loss figures or before-and-after results break most platform rules and many laws.

steps.p: A conversion does not turn into money the moment it happens. It moves through stages, and each one takes time. Knowing these stages stops you from panicking, or overspending, while you wait to be paid.
steps.more: Pending means the conversion has been recorded but not yet checked. Validation is when the advertiser reviews it for fraud, duplicates, wrong geos and reversed deposits. Approved means it passed and will be paid. Rejected means it failed and will not be paid. The network then pays approved earnings on its schedule, often after a billing period closes. Money can then take extra days to arrive depending on the payment method. Your dashboard total is not cash until it is in your account.

steps.say: Payment terms tell you when approved money is sent. Look at the table. Net seven, net fifteen and net thirty mean you're paid seven, fifteen or thirty days after the period closes. steps.h: Why cash runs out while you are winning
steps.p: Example: you spend $300 a week and earn $360 a week in payouts, a 20% return. Payouts arrive about four weeks after the spend. By week seven you have spent $2,100 and received only $1,080, even though the campaign is profitable.
steps.more: This is called a cash-flow gap. Spend leaves your account every day, but payouts come back weeks later after holds and payment terms. The gap is largest in the first month, then stays roughly constant while you keep spending at the same level. If you increase your budget, the gap grows too. Many new buyers stop profitable campaigns, or borrow money, because they did not plan for this. Treat the gap as part of the capital the campaign needs. All figures here are an example.

By week seven, you've spent two thousand one hundred dollars and received only one thousand and eighty, even though the campaign is profitable. steps.h: How much cash to keep in reserve
steps.p: A simple rule: keep enough money to cover your daily spend for the whole time between spending and getting paid, plus a buffer. Example: $40 a day, 30 days until the first payment arrives, plus a 20% buffer comes to $1,440.

Example: forty dollars a day, times thirty days until the first payment, plus a twenty percent buffer, comes to one thousand four hundred and forty dollars. steps.p: Some conversions are rejected after review. Common reasons are duplicate users, users from geos the offer does not accept, banned traffic types, refunded deposits and suspected fraud. A small rejection rate is normal. A sudden large one needs a written explanation.
steps.more: Rejecting invalid conversions is called a scrub. It is a normal part of the business, because advertisers do not pay for users who do not meet the terms. A clawback is when a conversion that was already paid is reversed later, for example after a chargeback, and deducted from your next payment. A shave is when a network or advertiser under-reports valid conversions on purpose. Shaving is hard to prove, which is why you keep your own records of clicks, sign-ups and deposits and compare them with the dashboard.

steps.h: An offer page is a contract

steps.p: Most offer pages share these fields, though the names and layout vary between networks. If a field is missing, ask your affiliate manager before you start. Missing information is your risk, not the network's.
steps.say: Here's the anatomy of an offer page. Payout gives the amount and model, per geo. Geos are the countries you may target. Allowed traffic lists the sources you may use. Restrictions say what's banned. Caps are the maximum paid results per period. K P Is are the quality bar users must meet. And the conversion flow is what the user must do. Names vary between networks. If a field is missing, ask your manager, because missing information is your risk, not the network's.

steps.h: Geos: where the user must be
steps.p: Geo is short for geography: the countries where users must be located. Payouts are set per geo, so the same offer can pay very different amounts in Kenya and in Germany. Conversions from outside the listed geos are usually rejected, even if the user deposits.
steps.more: Networks often group countries into tiers. Tier 1 usually means high-income markets with expensive traffic and high payouts. Tier 2 and Tier 3 cover middle- and lower-income markets with cheaper traffic and lower payouts. The tiers are informal and differ between networks. Geo is usually detected from the user's IP address and the details they give during sign-up. If many of your users appear to come from an unlisted country, check your ad targeting first. The geo strategy module in School 2 covers this in depth.

d.s: Users outside the list are not paid

steps.say: Geo is short for geography: the countries where users must be located. Payouts are set per geo, so the same offer can pay very different amounts in Kenya and in Germany. Conversions from outside the listed geos are usually rejected, even if the user deposits. Networks often group countries into tiers by income and traffic cost, but tiers are informal. If many users seem to come from an unlisted country, check your ad targeting first.

steps.p: Offers list which traffic types you may use. Using a banned source is one of the most common reasons a whole month of conversions gets rejected. Lists differ between offers, so check each one. These are typical examples.
steps.more: Incentivised traffic means paying or rewarding users to sign up or deposit, for example offering airtime or cash for registering. Advertisers ban it because those users rarely stay. Brand bidding means running search ads on the advertiser's own brand name, which competes with the advertiser's own ads. Misleading creatives include fake news articles, fake celebrity endorsements and promises of guaranteed profit. If you are unsure whether a source is allowed, ask your manager and keep the reply.

steps.h: Caps: the ceiling on paid results
steps.p: A cap is the maximum number of conversions the advertiser will pay for in a period, often per day, week or month, and sometimes per geo. Results above the cap may be unpaid or paid at a lower rate. Ask your manager about the cap before you raise spend.

d.s: Over the cap can mean unpaid

steps.say: A cap is the ceiling on paid results. It's the maximum number of conversions the advertiser will pay for in a period, often per day, week or month, and sometimes per geo. Results above the cap may be unpaid, or paid at a lower rate. So ask your manager about the cap before you raise spend.

steps.p: Example: an offer has a daily cap of 10 FTDs at $50. On a good day your campaign brings 14. If the terms say conversions over the cap are not paid, the money you spent to get those extra 4 earned you nothing.

d.text: 14 FTDs, cap of 10: 10 × $50 = $500 paid. The 4 extra were bought and not paid. Ask before you scale.

steps.say: Here's what hitting a cap looks like. Example: an offer has a daily cap of ten F T Ds, first-time deposits, at fifty dollars. On a good day, your campaign brings fourteen. If the terms say conversions over the cap aren't paid, you get ten times fifty, five hundred dollars. The money you spent to get those extra four earned you nothing. Ask before you scale.

steps.p: KPI means key performance indicator. On an offer page, KPIs are the quality rules your users must meet, such as a minimum deposit or a share who verify their identity. Miss them and the advertiser may cut your payout, pause you or reject conversions.
steps.more: KPIs exist because an advertiser's real goal is customers who stay, not one-off sign-ups. If your users deposit the minimum and never return, the advertiser loses money on your CPA. KPIs are usually measured across all your users over a period, such as a week or month, rather than one by one. That means a single bad traffic source can drag down your whole account. Ask your manager how KPIs are measured, over what period, and what happens if you miss them.

steps.p: The conversion flow is what a user must do for you to be paid. A longer flow converts fewer people. Walk through it yourself on your phone, up to the payment step, so your ads describe the steps honestly.

A longer flow converts fewer people. So walk through it yourself on your phone, up to the payment step, and make sure your ads describe those steps honestly.

steps.h: What is one sign-up worth to you?
steps.p: To compare offers fairly, estimate the value of one sign-up. Multiply the payout by the share of sign-ups who deposit. Your manager may share a rough rate for your geo. Example: $60 payout × 5% deposit rate = $3 per sign-up.
steps.more: This number is your ceiling. If one sign-up is worth $3 to you, paying more than $3 to get it loses money, and paying $2 leaves $1 of margin. Treat any rate your manager gives as a starting estimate, because your traffic may convert better or worse than average. The numbers module teaches the full set of numbers, including earnings per click and break-even, and shows how to replace estimates with your own data.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll learn to read an offer page like a contract: payout, geos, allowed traffic, caps, K P Is and the conversion flow. Then you'll compare offers by what one sign-up is worth and choose a sensible first offer.
lessons.say_outro: So, read the whole offer page as a contract, check caps, geos, allowed traffic and K P Is, and compare offers by value per sign-up, not headline payout. Your task: choose two offers, fill in payout, geos, allowed traffic, cap, K P Is and conversion flow for each, estimate value per sign-up, and pick one as your first offer. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: You spent $400 this week. The dashboard shows 10 conversions at $45: 8 approved and 2 pending. What is your confirmed profit so far?
exam.why: Only approved conversions count: 8 × $45 = $360. $360 − $400 = −$40. The 2 pending may or may not be approved.

exam.q: You have $500 and want to keep testing for two months. A network offers $40 CPA or 35% lifetime RevShare on the same offer. Which fits best and why?
options: RevShare, because lifetime always pays more
CPA, because cash returns sooner and funds the next tests
RevShare, because it has no KPIs
Neither, because the budget is too small to start
exam.why: With a small budget you need cash back quickly. CPA pays a known amount after approval, while RevShare builds slowly and may be low or negative early on.

exam.q: A trading offer pays well in a country where you are not sure retail trading ads are allowed on your platform. What should you do before spending?
options: Launch with a small budget and see if the ad is approved
Write the ad without mentioning trading
Check the platform's current financial services policy and local law, and confirm the broker's licence with your manager
Target a nearby country instead and hope users travel
exam.why: Regulated verticals need checks first: platform policy, local law and the advertiser's licence. Hiding what you advertise is circumvention and breaks policy.

exam.q: Example: you plan $60 a day. Your network pays Net 30 after a monthly period, so your first payment arrives about 60 days after you start. You have $2,500 set aside. Using the 20% buffer rule, what should you do?
options: Start at $60 a day; the money will come
Lower the daily spend to about $34 a day, which the reserve covers
Borrow the difference
Spend it all in the first week to get data faster
exam.why: $60 × 60 days × 1.2 = $4,320 needed, more than $2,500. $2,500 ÷ (60 × 1.2) ≈ $34.70, so about $34 a day fits: $34 × 60 × 1.2 = $2,448. Never borrow to fund a test.

exam.q: Your campaign brings 25 FTDs in one day. The offer cap is 15 per day and extra FTDs are not paid. What is the right next step?
options: Keep spending, the network will pay anyway
Pause the campaign at the cap each day and ask the manager for a higher cap before scaling
Send the extra users to the same offer through another network
Delete the campaign
exam.why: Spend above the cap buys unpaid conversions. Control spend to the cap and request a higher one in writing before you scale.

exam.q: Offer A pays $90 with an estimated 2% sign-up to FTD rate. Offer B pays $55 with 4%. You can buy sign-ups at about $1.80. Which offer is profitable at that price?
options: Only Offer A
Neither
Both equally
Only Offer B
exam.why: A is worth $90 × 2% = $1.80 per sign-up, so you break even. B is worth $55 × 4% = $2.20, leaving $0.40 margin per sign-up.

exam.q: A friend says you can boost FTDs by giving users ₦2,000 airtime for depositing. The offer bans incentivised traffic. What happens if you do it?
options: Conversions will likely be rejected and you may lose the offer
You will be paid a bonus for creativity
Nothing, if the deposit is real
Your payout will rise because users are happier
exam.why: Rewarding deposits is incentivised traffic. Advertisers detect it, reject the conversions and can remove you from the offer.

exam.q: You are applying to your first network. You have never run ads. Which answer to "Describe your experience" is best?
options: "5 years, $10k a day on Meta" so they approve you
Leave it blank
"New. Plan: COD e-commerce in Ghana on Meta, about $25 a day. Completed a media buying course."
"Experienced. Will share stats later."
exam.why: Honest and specific answers get approved and get useful offers. Invented experience is exposed by your traffic quality within days and can close the account.

exam.q: A new network promises $150 per FTD, triple everyone else, and asks for a $50 activation fee. Which response is best?
options: Pay quickly before the offer ends
Treat it as a warning sign, decline, and stick to established networks
Pay with a borrowed card
Ask them to deduct the fee from your first payment
exam.why: Payouts far above the market plus a fee to join are classic scam signs. Legitimate networks are paid by advertisers, not affiliates.

exam.q: A nutra offer pays $30 per confirmed order. A colleague suggests the hook 'Doctors hate this: cures diabetes in 30 days'. What do you do?
options: Use it, since it gets attention
Use it only in countries without health laws
Reject the hook: it is a false health claim and a fake authority angle, and write an honest one about what the product is
Use it but add small print
exam.why: Disease cure claims and fake authority break platform rules and many laws. Small print does not fix a misleading headline.
